title: A Considerable Speck
author: Robert Frost
tagline: Poem · gently humorous · respect for a tiny creature and for the mind within it

overview.intro: A poet is writing when a tiny creature, barely more than a speck, crawls across his page. He watches it and expects to brush it aside, but he notices that it reacts sensibly to the fresh, wet ink, pausing and turning away as if it can think and choose. That sign of intelligence changes his attitude. Where he might have crushed it, he now feels respect, because he recognises a mind at work in something so small. He spares it, and the poem ends with a quiet, humorous statement about respecting minds wherever we find them.

learn.title: What the poem says, stage by stage

blocks.text: This is a broad paraphrase in our own words. Read the poem in your textbook and match each stage to the lines.

items: Stage 1 (the setting): the poet is at his writing, with his page in front of him. He is absorbed in his work.
Stage 2 (the visitor): a tiny creature appears and starts to move across the paper. It is so small that it seems only a speck, and it is natural to think of it as a nuisance, or as nothing at all.
Stage 3 (the reaction to ink): as it crawls, the creature comes near wet ink and reacts to it. It stops, changes direction, or avoids it, as though it understands that it is unsafe.

Stage 4 (the realisation): the poet sees that this is more than blind movement. It looks like judgement, and even fear. He concludes that there must be a mind in the small body, a mind that wants to go on living.
Stage 5 (the decision): instead of killing it, he lets it be. His respect for a mind, even in the smallest creature, stops him.

Stage 6 (the closing thought): the poem ends on a lightly humorous but sincere note. The poet says that he recognises a mind when he meets one, in whatever form, and that a creature with such a mind has nothing to fear from him.

blocks.text: Intelligence and the will to live deserve respect wherever they are found, even in the tiniest and most unimportant-looking creature. The poet's kindness comes not from sentiment but from recognising something like himself in the speck: a mind that thinks and chooses.
The poem also suggests, gently, that human beings are not the only creatures with minds, and that size is not a measure of worth.

items: Tone: light, amused and conversational. The poet talks about a tiny insect as though it were a fellow thinker, with mild humour.
Mood: thoughtful and warm. The reader shares the poet's surprise and his growing respect.
Underneath the humour there is a serious moral point about compassion and about respecting life in every form.

items.meaning: The poet treats an event no bigger than a crawling speck as important, and even the title jokes that the speck is 'considerable'. The contrast between the tiny creature and the large idea creates gentle comedy.
The creature is described as having thoughts and choices, like a person who decides to stop and turn. This prepares the reader for the poet's claim that it has a mind.
A creature that seems to deserve no attention teaches the writer to think about the nature of mind, and a human who could easily crush it is the one who shows restraint.
The speaker addresses us directly in ordinary speech, which makes the poem feel personal and the ideas easy to accept.
The wet ink stands for danger and the page for the poet's world of thought. The creature crossing it shows two minds meeting on the same ground.

items: State clearly what makes the poet change his attitude: the creature's sensible reaction to the wet ink.
Do not say that the poet spares the creature only out of pity. It is respect for a mind.
Explain the title. It is humorous because a speck is by definition tiny, yet the poet finds it important enough to write about.
Mention both the humorous tone and the serious message when writing about the poem as a whole.

keyPoints: The poet is writing when a tiny creature crawls across his page.
The creature reacts to the wet ink by pausing and avoiding it.
This shows the poet that the speck has a mind and a wish to live.
He spares it out of respect for that mind.
The poem is humorous in tone but carries a serious message about respecting life.

questions.prompt: Where does the tiny creature crawl in the poem?
options: Up the wall of his room
questions.explanation: The poet is at his desk, and the creature crosses the page on which he is writing.

questions.prompt: What behaviour of the creature convinces the poet that it has a mind?
options: It runs away when he speaks
It stops and avoids the wet ink
It follows the movement of his pen
questions.answer: It stops and avoids the wet ink.
questions.explanation: The creature's careful reaction to the ink looks like sensible judgement, not blind motion.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking it reacts to the poet himself.

questions.prompt: Which of these best describes the tone of the poem?
options: Light and humorous, with a serious thought underneath
questions.answer: Light and humorous, with a serious thought underneath.
questions.explanation: The joking treatment of a tiny creature carries a serious message about respecting minds and life.
questions.commonMistake: Ignoring the humour, or ignoring the serious point.

questions.prompt: Describe what the poet sees happening on his page.
questions.answer: A very small creature is crawling across the paper. As it moves, it comes close to the wet ink, and the poet sees it stop and turn or draw back as if it knows that the ink is dangerous. This makes him watch it closely.
questions.explanation: Mention the creature's movement and its reaction to the ink.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the creature drowns in the ink.

questions.prompt: Why does the poet decide not to harm the tiny creature?
questions.answer: The poet sees that the creature reacts sensibly to danger, and from this he concludes that it has a mind and a wish to live. He recognises something like himself in it and feels respect for that mind, however small the body that holds it. Because of this he chooses to spare it instead of crushing it.
questions.explanation: State what he observes, what he concludes and what he decides.
questions.commonMistake: Saying he spares it only because he is tired or busy.

questions.prompt: Explain why the title of the poem is humorous and appropriate.
questions.answer: A speck is by definition tiny and unimportant, so calling it considerable is a joke, and it is a mild exaggeration in the opposite direction. The title is appropriate because the poet ends up treating the speck as important. It deserves attention and respect because it has a mind, so the small creature turns out to be considerable in the way that matters.
questions.explanation: Explain the contrast in the title and link it to the poet's change of view.
questions.commonMistake: Explaining only the meaning of the word speck.

questions.prompt: How does the poet's attitude towards the creature change between the beginning and the end of the poem?
questions.answer: At first the creature is only a speck on his page, a small interruption that he could brush away or ignore. As he watches it react to the wet ink, he begins to take an interest and to see signs of thought in its movements. By the end he has developed respect for it, seeing in it a mind that wants to live, and he spares it and treats it almost as an equal. The change moves from indifference to curiosity and then to respect, and the poem shows this change as a small lesson in humility.
questions.explanation: Describe three stages (indifference, curiosity, respect) and give the cause of the change.
questions.commonMistake: Describing the ending without the starting attitude.

questions.prompt: The poem treats a small event lightly but expresses a serious idea. Discuss how humour and seriousness work together in 'A Considerable Speck'.
questions.answer: The humour comes from the contrast between the tiny creature and the large amount of thought it receives. The poet talks about a speck as if it were a thinker, and the title itself is a joke. Yet the humour does not cancel the message. Behind the joke is the serious idea that intelligence and the wish to live deserve respect wherever they appear, and that size is no guide to worth. The light tone makes the idea easy to accept, because the reader is smiling and not being lectured. The poet also teaches by example: he acts with restraint towards a creature he could easily destroy. Humour and seriousness together give a gentle moral that stays in the mind because it is not preached.
questions.explanation: Explain the source of the humour, the serious idea, and how the combination affects the reader.
questions.commonMistake: Treating the poem as either a joke or a sermon.

questions.prompt: The poet spares the creature because he recognises a mind in it. Do you think we should respect living things only when they show signs of intelligence? Give reasons for your view.
questions.answer: I think intelligence is one good reason for respect, and the poet is right to be moved by it, but it should not be the only reason. Many living things show little sign of thought and yet can suffer, and a caring person would spare them too. The poem, however, does not claim that only clever creatures matter. It shows how noticing thought in a small creature can change our attitude, and this can be the start of a wider kindness. So the poem invites us to look more closely at living things before we dismiss them, while I would add that basic respect for life should not depend on proof of intelligence.
questions.explanation: Any reasoned view is acceptable. Give a clear position, refer to the poet's reasoning, and consider the opposite view.
questions.commonMistake: Agreeing or disagreeing without reference to the poem.

questions.prompt: Identify two poetic devices used in 'A Considerable Speck' and explain the effect of each.
questions.answer: Personification: the creature is shown thinking and making choices, so the reader accepts the idea that it has a mind. Irony: a creature that appears insignificant becomes the subject of serious thought, and the person with power over it chooses restraint. Both devices support the poem's gentle humour and its message of respect for life.
questions.explanation: Name each device, say how it appears in the poem in your own words, and state its effect.
questions.commonMistake: Naming devices with no reference to the poem.
